rewrites.summary:
This division sits under the national framework: no division-specific trans law, enforcement series or incident pattern was found in the research pass, so the legal protections a visiting trans person stands under are the national ones. Those are in mid-flux: parliament passed an amendment in March 2026 (assent pending) that removes the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricts legal recognition to traditionally recognised groups (hijra/kinner) and intersex people, and makes medical certification a condition of identity recognition — a direct documents consequence for a trans traveler whose papers rest on that certification.

The amendment also adds a coercion offence carrying up to life imprisonment for 'coercing or alluring' anyone to be transgender, which the human-rights reporting warns could criminalise support networks — the main new criminal exposure a visitor brushing against advocacy or trans peer groups could face. No deviation from the national position was material enough to score separately (±0.02); the division is assessed at the national score.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National policy turbulence colours the visit without being local risk: the amendment reversed the 2014 rights position over warnings from a court-appointed advisory panel and critics that it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people; the human-rights organisation urged that it not be signed, and protests followed the vote in several cities. A civil-liberties group warns the new coercion offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. No division-specific litigation or comparisons with neighbouring divisions are documented.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing content: this division is not among the handful of units that constituted the mandated transgender welfare board, and its protective policy depends on the national government — a documented driver of the welfare-board gap. The government says the narrower definition targets welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection for residents. The sourced claims also carry nationwide resident data: the census records 487,803 transgender people but only about 32,500 hold identity cards, and the broader estimate reaches around two million.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Whether the amendment becomes law is unresolved: assent was pending as of late March 2026. No division-specific trans statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file, and no border or entry-document practice specific to this division beyond the national medical-certification mandate is recorded.
